paper_title: DLP Dynamic Layerwise Pruning in Large Language Models
caption: Comparison of per-output and per-layer perplexity at different sparsity rates. Due to the significant difference in values between high and low sparsity rates, we use the logarithmic results for comparison.

model_annotations.Bulgarian: The bar chart illustrates a comparison between “Per-Output” and “Per-Layer” pruning strategies in terms of perplexity across varying sparsity rates, ranging from 10% to 80%, as presented in the paper “DLP Dynamic Layerwise Pruning in Large Language Models.” The horizontal axis (x-axis) represents the sparsity rate as a percentage, labeled at intervals of 10%, while the vertical axis (y-axis) displays perplexity on a logarithmic scale, spanning from 10¹ to 10³, with major gridlines at powers of ten. Two distinct bar colors are used: blue for “Per-Output” and orange for “Per-Layer,” as indicated in the legend positioned in the upper left corner. At lower sparsity rates (10%–50%), both strategies yield similarly low perplexity values, visually clustered near the 10¹ level. As sparsity increases beyond 50%, perplexity rises sharply for both methods, with “Per-Layer” consistently exhibiting slightly higher perplexity than “Per-Output” at 60%, 70%, and 80%. At 80% sparsity, both bars reach their maximum heights, with “Per-Output” at approximately 500 and “Per-Layer” exceeding 700, both still within the 10² to 10³ range. The chart uses a logarithmic y-axis to accommodate the wide range of perplexity values, particularly to make the differences at lower sparsity rates visually discernible despite the large magnitude increase at higher sparsity. No bars are grouped or stacked; each sparsity level has two adjacent bars representing the two pruning methods, and all bars are uniformly spaced and aligned with their respective x-axis labels.
model_annotations.Chinese: This bar chart compares the perplexity of two pruning strategies—“Per-Output” (blue) and “Per-Layer” (orange)—across eight different sparsity rates ranging from 10% to 80%, as evaluated in the context of dynamic layerwise pruning in large language models. The horizontal axis represents the sparsity rate as categorical labels (10%, 20%, ..., 80%) in ascending order, while the vertical axis displays perplexity on a logarithmic scale ranging from 10¹ to 10³, with major gridlines at 10¹, 10², and 10³. For each sparsity rate, two adjacent bars show the respective perplexity values for the two methods. At low sparsity rates (10%–50%), both methods exhibit low and nearly identical perplexity values, hovering just above 10¹. As sparsity increases beyond 50%, perplexity rises sharply for both methods, with the “Per-Layer” strategy consistently yielding higher perplexity than “Per-Output” at 60%, 70%, and 80%. At 80% sparsity, the “Per-Output” perplexity reaches approximately 500 (just below 10³), while “Per-Layer” exceeds 1000 (above 10³), indicating a more severe degradation in performance under aggressive pruning. The use of a logarithmic scale emphasizes the exponential growth in perplexity at higher sparsity levels, and no bars are visually emphasized through shading or annotations beyond their color-coded grouping.
model_annotations.English: The bar chart illustrates the comparison of perplexity values for two pruning strategies—“Per-Output” (blue bars) and “Per-Layer” (orange bars)—across eight different sparsity rates (10% to 80%) in large language models, as presented in the paper “DLP: Dynamic Layerwise Pruning.” The vertical axis, labeled “Perplexity,” is displayed on a logarithmic scale ranging from 10¹ to 10³, with major gridlines at 10, 100, and 1000, to accommodate the wide range of values and highlight differences more clearly. The horizontal axis lists sparsity rates in 10% increments from 10% to 80%. At low sparsity rates (10%–50%), both strategies yield very similar and low perplexity values, with bars clustered near 10¹. As sparsity increases to 60%, perplexity begins to rise slightly for both, with “Per-Layer” showing a marginally higher value. At 70% sparsity, “Per-Output” reaches approximately 15 and “Per-Layer” approximately 25. At 80% sparsity, perplexity increases sharply: “Per-Output” reaches approximately 400, while “Per-Layer” exceeds 600, indicating significantly higher model degradation under high sparsity for the per-layer approach. The chart visually emphasizes that while both methods perform similarly at low sparsity, the per-layer pruning incurs a greater cost in perplexity at higher sparsity levels.
model_annotations.German: Das Balkendiagramm vergleicht die Perplexität von zwei Pruning-Strategien — „Per-Output“ (dargestellt durch blaue Balken) und „Per-Layer“ (dargestellt durch orange Balken) — bei unterschiedlichen Sparsitätsraten, die auf der horizontalen Achse von 10 % bis 80 % in 10 %-Schritten angegeben sind. Die vertikale Achse zeigt die Perplexität auf einer logarithmischen Skala mit Werten von 10⁰ bis 10³, wobei die Tick-Markierungen bei 10⁰, 10¹, 10² und 10³ liegen und durch gestrichelte Linien gekennzeichnet sind. Bei jeder Sparsitätsrate sind zwei nebeneinander angeordnete Balken zu sehen, wobei der linke Balken die „Per-Output“-Strategie und der rechte die „Per-Layer“-Strategie repräsentiert. Bei niedrigen Sparsitätsraten (10 % bis 50 %) liegen beide Balken nahe bei 10⁰, wobei die „Per-Output“-Werte leicht niedriger sind. Ab 60 % Sparsität steigen beide Werte an, wobei der „Per-Layer“-Balken stärker ansteigt als der „Per-Output“-Balken. Bei 70 % Sparsität liegt der „Per-Output“-Wert bei etwa 10¹, während der „Per-Layer“-Wert knapp über 10¹ liegt. Bei 80 % Sparsität erreicht der „Per-Output“-Balken etwa 500 (zwischen 10² und 10³), während der „Per-Layer“-Balken über 1000 (nahe 10³) liegt. Die Balken sind nicht sortiert, sondern nach steigender Sparsitätsrate angeordnet, und es gibt keine visuellen Hervorhebungen außer der Farbcodierung gemäß der Legende oben links.
